contract: localize(spectrum) -> list of float. spectrum = {'subject': 'textwrap', 'urllib.parse' or 'fractions', 'blocks': n, 'failed': F, 'passed': P, 'ef': [n ints], 'ep': [n ints]} describes one faulty version of the module: F of its pool tests fail (their outcome differs from the correct module's) and P pass, and ef[b] (ep[b]) is the number of failing (passing) tests that execute block b, where blocks are the evaluator's block probes (function entries, branch outcomes, loop bodies and exits, handlers) in a random order that is drawn anew for every fault and every evaluation, so an index does not denote the same block in different faults or evaluations; the faults are presented in a random order as well. Return n finite numbers, a suspiciousness per block (higher means more likely faulty). Score: mean EXAM over the 532 faults, i.e. the faulty block's rank (ties count as their average rank) divided by n, minimised. localize() is called once per fault, all faults in one sandboxed subprocess (no files, network or subprocesses; 120 s CPU in total, 2 GB); it should be deterministic (seed any randomness, do not read clocks).
notes: Faults are the evaluator's first-order mutants of CPython 3.12.14's textwrap, urllib.parse and fractions (PSF licence), one fault per version, detected by a seeded 240-call test pool; spectra are block hit counts from the evaluator's own probes, and the faulty block is the statement-level block that contains the mutated statement. The literature mostly uses statement-level spectra of real or hand-seeded faults (Siemens, Defects4J), so absolute EXAM values are not comparable; Tarantula, Ochiai and DStar(2) are computed on the same data and reported in the details.

name: Software engineering: spectrum-based fault localisation of seeded faults in three CPython modules
description: Rank the code blocks of a faulty module by suspiciousness using only its program spectrum: for each block, how many failing and passing tests execute it. The 532 faults are first-order mutants of textwrap, urllib.parse and fractions; the score is the mean EXAM (rank of the faulty block divided by the number of blocks).
benchmark: Software engineering: spectrum-based fault localisation of seeded faults in three CPython modules
paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

sources.locator: Jones and Harrold (ASE 2005): the Tarantula fault-localisation technique and its evaluation by the share of code examined (the seed).
Abreu, Zoeteweij and van Gemund (TAIC PART 2007): accuracy of spectrum-based fault localisation with block hit spectra; Ochiai coefficient.
Wong, Debroy, Gao and Li (IEEE Trans. Reliability 2014): the DStar formula.
Yoo (SSBSE 2012): evolving risk-evaluation formulas with genetic programming, the program-search setting of this task.
Pearson et al. (ICSE 2017): results on artificial faults do not carry over to real faults; the main caveat of this task.
CPython 3.12.14 source release (PSF licence): textwrap, urllib.parse and fractions.

limitations: Faults are artificial first-order mutants, one per version; Pearson et al. (ICSE 2017) found that rankings of fault-localisation techniques on artificial faults do not predict their rankings on real faults.

Spectra are block hit counts from this evaluator's probes and a seeded 240-call test pool per module, not statement coverage of a project's own test suite; the faulty block is the statement-level block containing the mutated statement (faults on one-line compound statements are left out), so EXAM values are not comparable with published ones.
Undetected mutants and mutants that break the import are excluded; textwrap contributes 110 faults, urllib.parse 183 and fractions 239.

Reference values computed here: Tarantula (the seed) 0.0506, Ochiai 0.0268 and DStar(2) 0.0248 mean EXAM; ranking each faulty block first among blocks with an identical spectrum would give 0.0087, a bound for formulas of the counts that no single formula need reach.

Blocks and faults are shown in a random order that changes with every evaluation, so neither a position nor the number of the call carries information; the score of a formula of the counts does not depend on the order. The faults are public, however: a spectrum identifies its fault, and a search can still overfit this fault set.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Fault localisation: given a faulty program and the outcomes and coverage of its tests, point developers to the code most likely responsible for the failures.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Locating faults is one of the most expensive debugging activities; spectrum-based techniques that rank code by how strongly its execution correlates with failing tests are among the most studied approaches in software engineering and are used by automated repair tools.

papers.title: Empirical evaluation of the tarantula automatic fault-localization technique
papers.primary_goal: Locate faulty statements by ranking them with a suspiciousness computed from passing and failing test coverage.
papers.task_relation: The task asks for such a ranking from test coverage spectra; Tarantula is the seed.

papers.task_relation: The task uses block hit spectra and the same rank-based accuracy measure.
